title: Ramadan: the family
hook: iftars with family, children's first fasts

segments.voice: Yesterday, planning Ramadan: reading, prayer, charity, and rest, the column people forget. Your line: plan the month. Did your four lines make it onto paper? Today, the people around the table. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-nine.

A small toy made of wool. That's the object at the center of today. Al-Rubayyi' bint Mu'awwidh, a woman of Madinah, describes it in Sahih al-Bukhari. Her people fasted, she says, and had their small children fast too. And they made toys out of wool for them. When one of the children cried for food, they'd hand over the toy, and the child would play with it until it was time to break the fast. No lecture. No scolding. A toy, and a little longer to wait. Today: Ramadan at home, with the whole family.
screen: `A TOY MADE OF WOOL.` → `A CHILD CRIES FOR FOOD.` → `PLAY UNTIL SUNSET.`

segments.voice: First, be honest about the report. Al-Rubayyi' is speaking about the fast of Ashura, not Ramadan. But it gives a picture of how children were brought into a fast: gently, with play, alongside the adults. Children aren't required to fast before they come of age, as you met earlier on the path. So a child's first fast is practice, not duty. Some families start with half a day, or a fast that ends at lunch, and make a fuss of the child at sunset. Second, the moment the fast breaks. In al-Bukhari the Prophet, peace be upon him, says people will remain in good as long as they hurry to break the fast. No waiting around to prove something. When the sun goes down, you eat. And in a report in Abu Dawud, Anas describes how: with fresh dates before the prayer, and if there were none, dried dates, and if there were none, a few sips of water. So the iftar starts small and sweet, and for some families the big meal comes after. Third, the table itself. For some families, iftar is the one meal of the day when everyone is home at the same minute, because the sun decides the time, not anyone's schedule. Grandparents, cousins, the kid who just finished a half-day fast and wants everyone to know. Fourth, put the toy and the date side by side. Both are small. Both say the same thing: the fast is hard, and the family's job is to make it bearable, together, until the moment it's sweet.
screen: `A CHILD'S FAST IS PRACTICE.` · `HURRY TO BREAK THE FAST.` · `DATES, THEN WATER.` · `EVERYONE HOME AT ONE MINUTE.`

segments.voice: The practice: include a child. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a child in your life, a son or daughter, a niece, a neighbor's kid, or the child you once were. Think of one way they could share in something you care about, sized to them. Not the whole thing. A half portion. A job at the table. Handing out the dates. Saying the first thing at a meal. Picture their face when they're trusted with it. Hold that picture for a few breaths. If you pray, you can remember that child by name. The bell holds the time.
Ramadan. The month of fasting, kept at home around the iftar table, where children practice small fasts and the day breaks with dates. Today's word.
Your line: the family fasts. Today, give one child a real job in something you do, sized just right for them. Tomorrow, Ramadan: the mosque. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Muslim families gather for iftar at sunset during Ramadan, breaking the fast with dates and water as a report in Abu Dawud describes; children aren't required to fast before maturity, and some families let them practice with partial fasts.

fork.setup: you're a mother in Madinah. your small child is fasting with the family, and at midday starts crying for food. what do you do?
options: give them a toy of wool to play with until it's time to break the fast.
tell them fasting isn't for children and send them away.
fork.reveal: al-Rubayyi' says they made toys of wool and gave one to a crying child until it was time to break the fast.

original.note: Arabic: breaking the fast, and the meal at sunset.

trapdoor: what you thought: in Ramadan, everyone, children included, fasts all day.
what it means: adults fast; children practice gently, and the family's table at sunset holds it all together.
what a scholar hears: al-Rubayyi's toys of wool in al-Bukhari, the hadith on hurrying the iftar, and Anas on dates and water in Abu Dawud.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 1960 (al-Rubayyi' bint Mu'awwidh: children fasting, toys of wool)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1957 (people remain in good as long as they hasten the iftar)
Sunan Abu Dawud 2356 (Anas: fresh dates, then dried dates, then sips of water)

notes: Bukhari 1960 concerns the fast of Ashura; the script says so plainly and uses it only as a picture of bringing children into a fast.
'Some families start with half a day' describes a common custom without a textual source; confirm framing.
Confirm hadith numbers and paraphrases: Bukhari 1960, 1957; Abu Dawud 2356 (dates before praying).
Editor pass: 'the big meal comes after' framed as some families' custom (not in Abu Dawud 2356); dropped 'often' from howItsDone.
